heading: John 2: the wedding at Cana and the temple
lede: Three scenes: water turned into wine at a wedding in Cana, Jesus driving the traders out of the Jerusalem temple, and a short note on the signs he did at Passover. For each verse: which Greek manuscripts up to AD 900 preserve it, where they disagree, and which Latin manuscripts up to 900 carry it.
latin_note: From this chapter on, the Latin list follows the manuscript catalogue of the Vetus Latina Iohannes edition, which covers every Old Latin manuscript of John; early Vulgate books are added below it. The Latin matters most at 2:3, where several Old Latin manuscripts share Sinaiticus’s longer text.

verses.translation: On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.
Jesus and his disciples had also been invited to the wedding.
When the wine ran short, the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine.”
Jesus said to her, “What is that to me and to you, woman? My hour has not yet come.”
His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”
Six stone water jars stood there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding two or three measures.
Jesus said to them, “Fill the jars with water.” And they filled them to the brim.
He said to them, “Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast.” So they took it.
When the master of the feast tasted the water that had become wine, not knowing where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), he called the bridegroom
and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and the poorer wine once the guests have drunk freely. You have kept the good wine until now.”
Jesus did this, the first of his signs, at Cana in Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.
After this he went down to Capernaum with his mother, his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there a few days.
The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
In the temple he found people selling cattle, sheep and doves, and the money changers sitting there.
Making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and the cattle. He scattered the money changers’ coins and overturned their tables.
To those selling doves he said, “Take these things out of here! Stop making my Father’s house a house of trade.”
His disciples remembered that it is written, “Zeal for your house will consume me.”
verses.greek_where_variant: ὁ ζῆλος τοῦ οἴκου σου καταφάγεταί με

verses.translation: The Jews then said to him, “What sign can you show us for doing these things?”
Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
The Jews then said, “This temple has been under construction for forty-six years, and you will raise it up in three days?”
But he was speaking about the temple of his body.
So when he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
While he was in Jerusalem at the Passover festival, many believed in his name when they saw the signs he was doing.
But Jesus would not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people
and needed no one to testify about anyone; for he himself knew what was in a person.

readings.witnesses: 01 (first hand) · Old Latin, including a and j

variants.explanation: The longer text spells out what the short one implies. It is a typical ‘Western’ expansion, and its appearance in Sinaiticus is a good example of a finding by Gordon Fee (1968): in the first eight chapters of John, Sinaiticus often sides with ‘Western’ witnesses such as the Old Latin rather than with Vaticanus. The same great codex can carry different kinds of text in different parts of one book.

variants.label: “like” a whip
variants.title: A whip of cords, or something “like” a whip?

readings.english: something like a whip of cords

variants.explanation: Here the two earliest papyri carry the reading the modern text does not print. The small word ὡς (“like”) softens the scene: Jesus improvises something whip-like. Editors usually judge that scribes were more likely to add a word than drop it, so the shorter text is printed, but the strength of 𝔓66 and 𝔓75 keeps the question open. A good example of how ‘earliest’ and ‘printed’ are not always the same.

variants.explanation: John quotes Psalm 69:9 (68:10 in the Greek Bible), where the Greek Psalm has the past tense. The future tense in John turns the quotation into a prediction of what zeal for the temple will cost Jesus; the past tense in later manuscripts brings John back into line with the Psalm, another harmonisation. The witness lists here are the least checked on this page.

translation_sweep.question: “Woman, what is that to me and to you?”
translation_sweep.explanation: A Semitic idiom (found also in the Greek Old Testament, for example Judges 11:12 and 2 Kings 3:13) whose tone is hard to carry into English: renderings range from “what concern is that to you and to me?” to “why do you involve me?”. The address “woman” was not rude in Greek, though it sounds so in modern English. Both belong to the translation sweep.

translation_sweep.question: Ancient measures (metrētēs, about 39 litres)
translation_sweep.explanation: A metrētēs was a liquid measure of roughly 39 litres (about 10 US gallons), so each jar held something like 80 to 120 litres. Translations variously keep the ancient unit, convert it, or round it; the sweep will set one policy for ancient measures across the site.
